south-arabia-museum.title: Bible Lands Museum: The Pre-Islamic Civilization of South Arabia
south-arabia-museum.evidence: Museum essays on the separate kingdoms, centres, inscriptions and social institutions; absolute dynastic chronology remains debated.

south-arabia-epigraphy.title: Caravan Kingdoms: Yemen and the Ancient Incense Trade, National Museum of Asian Art
south-arabia-epigraphy.evidence: Museum overview of distinct South Arabian kingdoms and changing regional power. Commercial reach is not mapped as direct sovereignty.

nabataean-study.title: Contextualizing the Nabataeans: A Critical Reassessment of their History and Material Culture
nabataean-study.evidence: Academic reassessment of ancient narratives and material evidence, including the 312 BCE expeditions and the danger of projecting later Petra backward.

main.text: Ma’in is one of the distinct kingdoms of ancient South Arabia, not a generic desert tribe or a branch of a single Arabian state. Its homeland lies in the Jawf, while Minaean people and inscriptions also appear along wider commercial routes. In 278 BCE, the kingdom belongs to a competitive regional world where agricultural centres, temples and long-distance exchange reinforce political importance.
main.homeland: The South Arabian Jawf, centred on Qarnaw and related Minaean communities
main.politicalForm: A South Arabian kingdom with a distinctive inscriptional and commercial tradition

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: The Minaean kingdom developed within the older urban and inscriptional landscape of South Arabia. Its historical record includes royal, religious and commercial texts rather than a continuous narrative like those preserved for Rome. Relative sequences of rulers are often more secure than exact dates. A precise spring king should therefore not be invented to make the article resemble a Mediterranean dynastic history.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: Qarnaw and other Jawf centres connect cultivated land with routes through and beyond the region. Minaean language and inscriptions distinguish this tradition from neighbouring Sabaean, Qatabanian and Hadramitic settings. People conducting business abroad may maintain strong homeland connections. Their presence at another oasis is evidence of a network, not sufficient proof that Ma’in owns that settlement.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Royal authority, temples and organized communities form part of the kingdom’s internal structure. Agriculture and maintenance of productive landscapes are as important to social life as merchants travelling long distances. The exact balance among these institutions changes through time. The opening should not reduce the whole population to caravan traders or assign all commercial activity to a royal monopoly.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Saba, Qataban and other South Arabian powers provide nearby rivals and partners. Northern routes connect Minaean merchants with places such as Dadan, where a commercial community need not replace local authority. Interdependence can coexist with political competition. The reach of an inscriptional network therefore exceeds what can safely be described as directly governed territory.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: Spring 278 places Ma’in within a developed South Arabian political landscape whose detailed chronology remains partly reconstructed from inscriptions. Its distinct language, centres and institutions justify a separate identity. The strongest starting account combines regional kingship and productive homeland with wider connections, while leaving uncertain royal dates and foreign dependencies carefully qualified.

saba.text: Saba is an old South Arabian power, rooted in a productive landscape of settlements, irrigation and religious institutions. Its history is much more substantial than the later stories attached to the name Sheba. By 278 BCE, it belongs to a competitive regional system rather than an uncontested kingdom ruling the entire peninsula or owning every route that carries Arabian incense.
saba.homeland: The southwestern Arabian highlands and Ma’rib-associated heartland
saba.politicalForm: An established South Arabian kingdom with royal, temple and communal institutions

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: Sabaean inscriptions document royal activity, warfare, building and dedication over many generations. Earlier periods of expansion do not establish permanent control of every neighbouring kingdom. Titles and political relationships change through time, and exact royal chronology remains debated. The legendary Queen of Sheba cannot be treated as a historical ruler of the campaign’s opening generation.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: Ma’rib and its cultivated surroundings illustrate the importance of water management and organized labour. The landscape supports settled communities and agricultural production alongside exchange. Irrigation infrastructure developed through construction and repair over time, not one timeless engineering event. Sabaean language and religious traditions also distinguish the kingdom from the other South Arabian societies around it.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Kings, temples and organized communities share a historical landscape in which productive land and collective works matter politically. The exact distribution of authority in spring 278 is less clear than the general institutional tradition. Later centralized or unified South Arabian arrangements should not be imported whole. Nor should the kingdom’s inhabitants be reduced to one merchant class.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Qataban, Ma’in and Hadramawt are distinct neighbouring powers with their own interests. Trade can connect them while territorial rivalry divides them. Demand for Arabian products in distant markets helps explain wider connections, but commercial influence is not sovereignty over the whole route. Later Himyarite unification belongs to another period and does not define the starting political map.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: The opening presents Saba as an established regional kingdom with a strong agricultural and religious foundation. Its historical credibility rests on inscriptional and archaeological evidence, not on a fictional peninsula-wide empire. The precise spring ruler and every dependency remain qualified, while the kingdom’s distinct identity and long institutional history are substantially better supported.

hadramaut.text: Hadramawt is a separate South Arabian kingdom whose eastern position and connections distinguish it from Saba and Qataban. Shabwa is central to its historical geography, while incense-producing districts and routes help explain its wider significance. In 278 BCE, it should appear as a regional power with its own institutions, not as a generic extension of whichever neighbouring kingdom is largest.
hadramaut.homeland: Eastern South Arabia, with Shabwa and the Hadramawt valley setting
hadramaut.politicalForm: A distinct South Arabian kingdom with a Hadramitic inscriptional tradition

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: Royal and dedicatory inscriptions preserve a distinctive Hadramitic historical tradition. They do not form a complete year-by-year political narrative, and exact royal dates can be difficult to establish. The kingdom’s long existence should therefore be separated from claims about one precisely known opening ruler. Later conquest and incorporation into larger South Arabian states belong to subsequent developments.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: The Hadramawt valley and its approaches connect settlements, cultivated areas and routes toward productive districts farther east and south. Shabwa provides an important focal point in that network. Coastal access and inland connections need not fall under one uniform administrative arrangement. The circulation of incense also depends on intermediaries rather than proving ownership of every origin and destination.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Kingship, religious institutions and local communities contribute to the internal political landscape. Hadramitic language and inscriptional practices support a distinct identity within South Arabia. The economy cannot be reduced to royal export income alone: agricultural support, settlement life and access to water remain fundamental. Exact spring balances among royal and local authorities are incompletely documented.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Qataban and other South Arabian powers form the closest competitive setting, while wider connections reach maritime and overland markets. Exchange with distant consumers does not make the kingdom their dependency. Nor does the presence of similar goods in another region establish Hadramitic sovereignty there. Political control and commercial participation must remain separate in describing its external position.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: Spring 278 places Hadramawt among the established regional kingdoms of South Arabia. Its distinct homeland, language and institutional tradition give it substance beyond an incense-trade label. The opening should retain those foundations while acknowledging uncertain absolute chronology and avoiding later imperial relationships, invented rulers or a monopoly over the whole southern Arabian exchange system.

qataban.text: Qataban is a major participant in the competitive kingdoms of ancient South Arabia. Its centre at Timna and the Wadi Bayhan setting give it a homeland distinct from Saba and Hadramawt. Around 278 BCE, it belongs to an established world of cultivated valleys, temples and royal power, whose history cannot be reduced to a single generic Arabian culture or trade confederation.
qataban.homeland: South Arabia, especially the Wadi Bayhan and Timna setting
qataban.politicalForm: A South Arabian kingdom with a distinct Qatabanic political and inscriptional tradition

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: Qataban developed within a regional political landscape shaped by earlier expansion, rivalry and shifting supremacy. Inscriptions record kings and communal activity, while modern reconstruction supplies much of the absolute chronology. The kingdom’s importance during this broad period is more secure than the exact reign dates of every ruler. Later destruction or incorporation should not be treated as an inevitable opening condition.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: Timna and nearby communities occupy a landscape where cultivation and routes reinforce one another. Qatabanic inscriptions distinguish a specific local tradition rather than merely a dialect label attached to Sabaean rule. Productive valleys and water arrangements sustain the population. Long-distance exchange matters, but cannot explain every aspect of the kingdom’s society or political organization.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Royal authority operates alongside religious and communal institutions visible in the inscriptional record. Building, dedication and regulation reveal organized public life beyond the movement of caravans. The precise spring 278 distribution of authority is not completely recoverable. A general account of kingship is appropriate without manufacturing a named ruler, modern bureaucracy or detailed national economic system.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Relations with Saba, Ma’in and Hadramawt combine competition and connection. Routes carrying valuable products can cross political boundaries without giving one kingdom sovereignty over the entire network. Regional prominence also changes over time. The opening should not assume that an earlier or later moment of Qatabanian dominance applies equally to every neighbouring settlement in this exact spring.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: The starting picture is a substantial South Arabian kingdom with its own language, centres and political traditions. Its importance is not dependent on copying a Greek royal court or inventing a peninsula-wide empire. The historical account preserves a credible regional core while leaving precise dynastic dates, changing supremacy and disputed dependencies open to qualification.

nabataea.text: The Nabataeans are already a recognizable community before 278 BCE, but their familiar monumental kingdom developed over a longer period. The opening comes after their resistance to Antigonid attacks in 312. Their history combines mobility, knowledge of difficult country and commercial connections, while the later royal cityscape of Petra should not be projected intact into this earlier generation.
nabataea.homeland: The southern Levant and northwestern Arabian route-connected setting
nabataea.politicalForm: An organized Arabian community before the better-documented later Nabataean monarchy

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: Diodorus preserves an account of the expeditions sent against the Nabataeans by Antigonus and Demetrius in 312 BCE. It describes organized resistance and valuable connections, although its ethnographic portrait is shaped by Greek narrative interests. This gives the opening a genuine earlier political background without proving that every institution of the later kingdom is already established.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: Routes, water knowledge and access to defensible places help explain the regional setting. The Petra-associated landscape matters, but the famous surviving facades and mature urban monuments largely belong to later centuries. Mobile activity and local settlement are not mutually exclusive. The society should not be portrayed either as a completed Roman-era city-state or as people without durable places.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: The evidence supports collective organization and the ability to coordinate defence. It does not securely supply a named spring 278 king or the full later court. Later coinage and inscriptions illuminate subsequent monarchy rather than automatically filling the earlier gaps. Commercial activity is significant, but not every inhabitant must be imagined as a merchant or caravan leader.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Ptolemaic and Seleucid interests frame parts of the surrounding southern Levant and Near East. Participation in routes connecting Arabia and Mediterranean markets creates both opportunities and pressure. Trading through a district does not establish ownership of it. The earlier Antigonid conflict is historical background, not a reason to impose an identical starting war against every Macedonian successor power.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: Spring 278 presents an organized regional community with proven capacity for resistance and valuable local connections. It precedes the fullest documentation of Nabataean royal institutions and the best-known architecture of Petra. The opening therefore has a credible historical identity without requiring a speculative ruler, premature monumental capital or an empire encompassing every connected trade route.

lihyan.text: Lihyan belongs to the oasis world of Dadan in northwestern Arabia. Inscriptions provide direct evidence for local kingship, religious life and society, although the exact chronology of the kingdom’s phases remains debated. For 278 BCE, a distinct oasis-centred political community is more defensible than an expansive Arabian empire or the assumption that foreign merchants determine the allegiance of the town.
lihyan.homeland: Dadan and the al-Ula oasis region in northwestern Arabia
lihyan.politicalForm: An oasis-centred kingdom known through Dadanitic inscriptions; detailed chronology remains debated

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: The historical relationship between earlier Dadan and the Lihyanite kingdom is reconstructed largely through inscriptions and archaeology. Local writing preserves people and institutions that are not simply appendages of Greek narrative history. Scholars differ over parts of the absolute chronology. An opening account should therefore describe the established tradition while avoiding a falsely precise royal succession for this spring.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: Dadan’s oasis concentrates cultivation, water, settlement and religious activity along important routes. Its local Dadanitic tradition differs from the Minaean community also attested in the wider setting. Foreign merchants can live, dedicate and organize locally without replacing the indigenous political authority. That distinction is essential when interpreting inscriptions as evidence for cultural presence rather than territorial ownership.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Royal names and titles show that kingship is more than a modern guess, but assigning every inscription to an exact year is difficult. Religious institutions and local communities are also visible. The society should not be reduced to one trading company or a ruler’s caravan business. The opening retains local political substance without manufacturing a fully known court.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Connections extend toward South Arabia and the southern Levant, with different participants using overlapping routes. Ma’in’s commercial links do not automatically make Dadan a Minaean possession. Later Nabataean expansion belongs to a changing regional history and should not be applied as an accomplished opening annexation. Local control, merchant presence and wider influence remain separate questions.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: Spring 278 can reasonably retain Lihyan as a distinct oasis kingdom while qualifying its exact dynastic chronology and territorial reach. Its identity rests on local evidence, not merely on a place between better-known states. The historical account emphasizes the community’s own institutions and setting, while resisting the temptation to turn every commercial connection into a political dependency.

gerrha.text: Gerrha is associated with the wealth and connections of eastern Arabia, but its exact location and political organization remain debated. Ancient descriptions make it an important commercial place rather than a securely mapped peninsula-wide state. At the 278 BCE opening, a regional Gulf community is plausible, while the details of later accounts need to be kept separate from contemporary certainty.
gerrha.homeland: Eastern Arabia and the Arabian side of the Persian Gulf; exact site identification is debated
gerrha.politicalForm: A Gulf-connected commercial community whose precise early political structure is uncertain

sections.title: Origins and historical development
sections.text: Greek geographical traditions describe Gerrha in connection with Arabian commerce and routes. Strabo preserves earlier reports but writes much later than the opening. Identifying the ancient city with a specific archaeological site remains a scholarly question. A vivid account of wealth therefore cannot supply a complete founding narrative, exact royal genealogy or certain territorial extent for spring 278.

sections.title: Homeland and regional society
sections.text: Eastern Arabian oases and Gulf approaches connect agriculture, maritime movement and overland routes. A commercial centre depends on surrounding communities and intermediaries rather than existing in isolation. Similar goods or inscriptions across the region reveal connections, not automatically one state. The wider eastern Arabian cultural setting should not be merged indiscriminately with South Arabian kingdoms or all inland Arabian populations.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Organized exchange implies social institutions and local authority, but the surviving evidence does not securely establish a detailed opening constitution. A council, monarchy or merchant oligarchy should not be selected merely because each sounds plausible for a trading place. The article can describe the community’s economic setting while leaving the precise political form honestly unresolved.

sections.title: External relationships at the opening
sections.text: Connections reach Mesopotamia, the Gulf and Arabian interior routes, within a world affected by Seleucid power and regional communities. Commercial dealings do not by themselves establish tributary or sovereign relationships. The later expedition of Antiochus III belongs to a different generation. Its outcome cannot define either Gerrha’s opening obligations or an automatic war with the Seleucid kingdom.

sections.title: The Spring 278 BCE setting
sections.text: The opening preserves Gerrha’s regional and commercial importance without turning it into a fictional empire of every Gulf route. The most secure historical distinctions are between a connected settlement community, the uncertain location of its centre and the much less certain extent of direct rule. Later testimony enriches that picture while remaining clearly later evidence.
